Documentation.Summary:
This class is responsible for calculating damage from explosions
            It works by recursively raycasting from the point it needs to 
            calculate to the explosion center. It does two types of raycast, 
            3D DDA raycasts for traversing grids (ships, stations) and Havok 
            raycasts for traversing space between grids. For each block, it builds
            a stack of blocks that are between it and the explosion center and then
            calculates the damage for all blocks in this stack. 
            It early exits if it encounters a block that was already calculated.
Computes damage for all blocks assigned in constructor

Used to calculate damage for entities that are not grids
            Can be called even if ComputeDamagedBlocks was not called before, but it doesn't do any caching

Members.Name: RenderSpritesToTexture
Members.Signature: void Sandbox.Game.Components.MyRenderComponentScreenAreas.RenderSpritesToTexture(area, sprites, textureSize, aspectRatio, backgroundColor, backgroundAlpha)

Documentation.Summary:
Replaces a screen area's texture with raw pixels, bypassing the sprite pipeline entirely — no
            T:VRage.Game.GUI.TextPanel.MySprite list, no glyph-to-quad expansion and no offscreen render pass, just an upload. For
            content that is already an image (a rendered map, a decoded video frame) this is far cheaper than encoding it
            as sprites for M:Sandbox.Game.Components.MyRenderComponentScreenAreas.RenderSpritesToTexture(System.Int32,VRage.Collections.ListReader{VRage.Game.GUI.TextPanel.MySprite},VRageMath.Vector2I,VRageMath.Vector2,VRageMath.Color,System.Byte) to draw back into pixels.
            data is mip 0 alone: tightly packed, top-down, RGBA one byte per channel, at least
            textureSize worth of bytes (a larger pooled buffer is fine — the extra is ignored). The
            renderer rebuilds the mip chain and marks the texture ready. Unlike the sprite path there is no aspect-ratio
            correction, so the buffer must already be at the area's texture resolution.
            The area's generated texture must exist — see M:Sandbox.Game.Components.MyRenderComponentScreenAreas.CreateTexture(System.Int32,VRageMath.Vector2I).

Finds free place for objects defined by position and radius.
            StepSize is how fast to increase radius, 0.5f means by half radius.
            NOTE: Following method may have the following problems:
            1) CorrectSpawnLocation() should be always followed by a second test for
               IsShapePenetrating()
            
            2) First overlapping test may result in returning a colliding test sphere with a
               physics voxel map (case overlappedVoxelmap != null and not a planet)
            
            3) In second overlapping test, CorrectSpawnLocation() is testing from basePos.
               It should probably test from currentPos cause it's the one that is
               modified by external cycle
            
            4) In second overlapping test, CorrectSpawnLocation() may have found
               a safe position but that won't be spotted and the result will
               be corrupted by the external cycle

Server-side seeking and tracking logic for a T:Sandbox.Game.Weapons.MyMissile. Added at runtime only when the
            missile's ammo is a seeker type. Uses a lightweight flight model: it turns
            the missile's nose toward the stored target at a limited rate and lets the missile drive acceleration and
            speed along that nose. Registers its own update ticks with MyEntityComponentUpdater (priority 801),
            which runs after the missile's own after-simulation tick (MySector, priority 800): the missile's
            travel auto-orient therefore reads a one-frame-stale P:Sandbox.Game.EntityComponents.MySeekerMissileComponent.IsGuiding, which is harmless because the
            seeker overwrites the heading later in the same frame while guiding.

(Re)initializes the seeker for a fresh launch, caching the guidance parameters (cones stored as half-angle
            cosines, per-tick turn step in radians and its cosine) and clearing prior lock state. Cheap enough to call
            on every (re)spawn of a pooled missile.

Members.Name: SpawnBot
Members.Signature: long Sandbox.ModAPI.IMyNPCSpawnerSessionComponent.SpawnBot(botDefinitionId, position, direction, up, name = null, factionTag = null, weaponsContainerSubtype = null, lootContainerSubtype = null, chatMessageSetSubtype = null, squadGridEntityId = 0)

Documentation.Summary:
Spawns a bot of any type (HumanoidBot or AnimalBot) at a position. Call it on the server, from the update thread.
            The bot persists until it dies or is removed; it never despawns by distance. A lone combat bot reacts only to hits on itself.
            A humanoid bot given a squad grid joins that grid's squad: alerts from grid damage, hits on squad members and gunshots near
            the grid, cover from hostile turrets while a player is near, a leash to the grid and squad chat. The squad is created with
            its first bot and saved with the world; all its bots share that bot's faction, and it speaks from that bot's chat message set.
            A squad with no living bots takes the faction of the next bot. When the grid is closed or its NPC claim countdown
            expires, its bots stay as lone bots. Placement, seating and despawning are up to the caller. Overrides apply to this character only; a
            definition with RemoveAfterDeath false respawns without them.
            Spawns nothing and returns 0 on a client, off the update thread, for an unknown bot definition, faction tag or subtype,
            for any override or squad on a non-humanoid bot, for a squad grid that does not exist or has an encounter crew, for a
            faction other than the squad's, and when the bot limit refuses the spawn; every case but the client one is logged.
Documentation.Returns: Entity id of the bot's character, or 0 when nothing was spawned.

Parameters.Name: direction
Parameters.Description: Forward direction; zero, or parallel to up, lets the game choose one.

Parameters.Name: up
Parameters.Description: Up direction; zero uses the gravity at the position.

Parameters.Description: Display name; null or empty picks a random CharacterName definition, or the bot definition's display name when there is none.

Parameters.Name: factionTag
Parameters.Description: Tag of the faction the bot joins; also gives it the faction's skin, its suit colour when the definition has UseFactionColor, and its BotLootContainerType. Null for none.

Parameters.Name: lootContainerSubtype
Parameters.Description: Subtype of the ContainerTypeDefinition the loot is generated from, in place of the faction's. Null uses the faction's, or none without a faction.

Parameters.Name: chatMessageSetSubtype
Parameters.Description: Subtype of the NpcChatMessageSetDefinition the bot speaks from. Null keeps the definition's ChatMessageSet.

Parameters.Name: squadGridEntityId
Parameters.Description: Entity id of the grid whose squad the bot joins; 0 for a lone bot.

A GUI screen owned by a mod: a real entry in the game's screen stack, so it takes focus, starves
            gameplay of input while it is open, fades in and out with the game's transitions, and closes on Escape.Derive from this, override the callbacks you need, and call M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.Open. The screen itself is
            empty: draw its content from M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.OnDraw(System.Single) with T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceText and
            T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceSprite, left on the default F:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceLayer.BelowHud layer,
            which composites in place inside the screen. Multiply colours by the alpha passed to M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.OnDraw(System.Single)
            so the content fades with the screen, and hit test with
            M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpace.TryGetCursorPosition(VRageMath.Vector2@), whose coordinates are the ones the content was drawn at.
            Anything that has to stay inside a panel - a scrolling list, a progress fill - is clipped with
            M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpace.UsingScissorRectangle(VRageMath.RectangleF,Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceLayer).Because the screen carries no controls, it is a mouse and keyboard surface: a gamepad can close it
            but cannot point at anything, as pointing in this GUI is a matter of control focus.Everything here must be called from the update thread, and a screen never outlives its session.
Colour of the background panel, which is drawn only together with a P:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.Size.
Closes the screen with the usual fade out. M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.OnClosed(System.Boolean) arrives once the fade has finished.

Shows the game's own close button in the corner of the panel. Clicking it goes through

Closes the screen without a fade, delivering M:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen.OnClosed(System.Boolean) before returning.

Whether Escape and the gamepad cancel button close the screen. On by default; a screen that turns it off
            has to offer the player some other way out.

Whether the mouse cursor is drawn while this screen has focus. On by default, since a screen with
            nothing to point at is the unusual case.
Darkens whatever is behind the screen, the way the game's own full-screen menus do.

Whether the screen is drawn. False while it is hidden underneath a screen that hides the ones below it.

Converts between the two coordinate spaces used by T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceText and
            T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceSprite, for laying out content that mixes them, and reports the cursor position
            in those same coordinates for hit testing what a mod has drawn. It also clips drawing to a rectangle, which
            is what scrolling lists, progress fills and panels that content must not spill out of are built from.Normalized [0,1] is  a fraction of the window. It is relative to the game's safe GUI
            rectangle, which is a centred, roughly 4:3 area, so on a wide screen normalized 0 sits well inside the left
            edge. Pixel coordinates are true window pixels. Computing one from the other by multiplying by the viewport
            size is therefore wrong; use these methods.
The safe GUI rectangle in window pixels: the area normalized [0,1] maps onto.

Converts a normalized [0,1] size to pixels. Note X and Y scale by different amounts, because the safe
            GUI rectangle is not square, which is why an equal normalized X and Y is not square on screen.
Converts a normalized [0,1] position, relative to the safe GUI rectangle, to window pixels.

Documentation.Summary:
Clips everything drawn inside the returned scope to a normalized rectangle, so a list can scroll under
            a fixed frame, a bar can be filled by revealing a wider sprite, and text can run out of a panel without
            spilling over its edge. The game's own scrollable lists and text boxes are built the same way.
Documentation.Returns:
A scope to dispose once the clipped drawing is done. Always use it with using: a scope
            that is never disposed clips the rest of the frame, and is closed for you when the frame ends.

Parameters.Name: normalizedRectangle
Parameters.Description:
Area to keep, within [0,1] relative to the safe GUI rectangle. A
            rectangle with no area clips everything; nesting a second one keeps only what falls inside both.

Parameters.Name: layer
Parameters.Description:
Layer this applies to. It must be the layer the draws being clipped are on, since
            each layer is composited at its own point in the frame.

Documentation.Summary:
Selects at which point of the frame screen-space text and sprites are composited, which decides what
            they end up on top of.
Above everything, including open screens and tooltips.

Above the game HUD but below open screens such as the terminal. A layer decides ordering only, so
            this still draws while the HUD itself is hidden.
Above the 3D scene but below the game HUD. Cheapest option, as nothing needs to be buffered.

Draws textured quads in screen space through the game's sprite renderer, for backgrounds, icons, bars
            and gauges that accompany T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceText.Immediate mode: every call draws for a single frame, so call it every frame, from a session
            component's M:VRage.Game.Components.MySessionComponentBase.Draw for content over the game, or
            from the OnDraw of a T:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyModScreen for the content of a mod's own screen, where the layer
            should be left at F:Sandbox.ModAPI.MyScreenSpaceLayer.BelowHud so it composites inside that screen. Must be
            called from the update thread.Textures are named by the subtype id of a transparent material declared in TransparentMaterials.sbc,
            the same ids used for billboards, so a mod's own textures need no extra setup beyond that definition.
            An id matching no such material is looked up as an LCD texture, which covers the whole set an LCD or a
            Programmable Block can draw, item and faction icons included, then as a GUI texture, which is what the
            game's own HUD and screens are built from, then as the icon of the definition named "TypeId/SubtypeId",
            which is what reaches block icons, and finally as the P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTexture.Name
            of a texture the mod is drawing into itself.

Indicates number of max messages waiting in queue before the oldest one will be dropped to make space for new one.

Whenever given message provider obtains new message respective programmable block gets called with provided argument.
            Each raised callback argument will be called only once per simulation tick no matter how many messages are there pending to be accepted.
            At most a single callback will be invoked each tick
            ==> If there are messages pending in multiple message providers with registered callback, one will be randomly picked and invoked. Rest will be deferred to the next tick and follow the same process.
            In case you don't consume all messages pending in given message provider, the callback will not be raise again in following tick unless new message arrives.

D3D12 debug layer (DX12 backend bring-up). Costs real frame time — validation runs on every API call and every
            stored message is marshalled out in DrainDebugMessages — so turn it off when measuring frame time and
            back on when bringing up a new pass family. Must be set before device creation to have any effect.

Diagnostic: report every CPU write to a buffer the GPU may still be reading — a write whose target was last
            bound by a frame the GPU has not finished. Unlike the discard-map tally this covers all write paths and
            reports the race actually happening rather than the buffer merely being at risk, and unlike
            F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.DX12SerializeFrames it does not perturb timing, so it can catch an artifact that only appears
            at full speed. Never ship it on.

Diagnostic: report a buffer WriteDiscard-mapped more than once in a frame on the path where discard
            renaming does not apply, where the second map overwrites what the draws recorded after the first still read.
            The only detector for that corruption — F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.DX12DetectCrossFrameWrites sees the cross-frame race
            instead. Turn it off when profiling/release: the tally takes a backend-wide lock on every
            such map, and the recording threads map in parallel.

DirectStorage file-to-GPU texture uploads. Cleared by the -nodirectstorage command line switch, which
            also keeps dstorage.dll from being loaded at all — the escape hatch for when the runtime itself is
            suspect. Must be set before device creation to stop the uploader from being created; flipping it later only
            steers subsequent loads back onto the CPU path.

Debug-only DirectStorage interop smoke test: right after D3D12 device creation, DStorage-read one content
            DDS into memory and byte-compare against File.ReadAllBytes, logging [DStorage] PASSED/FAILED. Proves the
            whole interop layer (factory, file, queue, request struct layout, status array, fence signal) with no
            renderer integration. Compiled out of Release entirely.

D3D12 GPU-based validation. Instruments the shaders, so out-of-bounds descriptor-table reads, uninitialised
            descriptors and wrong resource states are named in the log instead of surfacing as a bare
            DXGI_ERROR_DEVICE_HUNG. Drastically slower — turn on only to diagnose a GPU fault, and expect the
            slowdown itself to change frame timings. Requires F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.DX12DebugLayer; must be set before device creation.

One-shot request (Ctrl+Shift+M) to stamp the render log with the current frame number and per-frame
            counters, so a visually-spotted artifact can be located in continuously-running traces. Set from the game
            thread, cleared by the render thread when it services it.

Measurement scaffold for the bindless-material plan: splits per-draw material SRV binds by binding pipeline and
            by merge-instancing, tracks the distinct material descriptors a session needs, and times the ring staging.
            See MyMaterialBindStats. Costs a timestamp pair per staged block plus a hash insert per material
            descriptor, so the timing it reports is very slightly inflated by its own measurement — turn it off before
            quoting absolute frame times. Temporary; remove with the scaffold.

Diagnostic: block in Present until the GPU has finished the whole frame, removing all CPU/GPU overlap
            while leaving parallel recording intact. Discriminates a cross-frame write-under-read (a buffer rewritten by
            frame N+1 while frame N's draws still read it) from a recording race — the former disappears here, the latter
            does not. Halves throughput; never ship it on.

Diagnostic: log the per-second VRAM breakdown (file textures, buffer pools, unaccounted). Off by default because
            each line walks every registered texture and pool on the render thread and adds ~350 lines per five minutes
            of log. Peaks, the sampler thread and the over-budget warning stay on regardless.

GPU debug markers: a BeginEvent/EndEvent region around every RHI profiling block, so a PIX/Nsight/RenderDoc
            capture reads as named passes instead of a flat draw list. Separate from F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.PerformanceProfiling
            because that also collects timestamps and is only reachable in a RELEASE_PROFILE build, which the DX12
            renderer has no buildable configuration for.

F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.ProfileFromStart for F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.RenderProfiling: collect from the first frame instead of
            waiting for the profiler to be opened (Alt+Decimal) and unpaused (Alt+Enter) by hand.

Render-only profiling. Keeps the profiler call sites of the render assemblies alive — the render thread's CPU
            blocks and the GPU timestamp blocks — while every game-side one stays compiled out, so DX12 can be profiled
            without F:VRage.MyCompilationSymbols.PerformanceProfiling, whose whole-game instrumentation costs a dictionary lookup and a
            timestamp on every block in the simulation and which the DX12 renderer has no buildable configuration for.
            Works because the symbol is only in the render projects' DefineConstants, and [Conditional] is
            resolved against the caller's defines.

A texture whose pixels a mod writes itself, created through M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTextures.Create(System.String,VRageMath.Vector2I,VRage.Game.ModAPI.MyGeneratedTextureFormat). Give
            P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTexture.Name anywhere the game takes a texture path — an LCD sprite of type
            VRage.Game.GUI.TextPanel.SpriteType.TEXTURE, for instance — and the renderer resolves it to this texture.
            Content that is already an image, such as a rendered map or a decoded video frame, costs one upload here against
            one textured quad per pixel if it were encoded as sprites for the panel to draw back into pixels.

Borrows a P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTexture.ByteCount-byte buffer to write the next image into. Fill it, then hand it to
            M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTexture.EndUpdate(System.Byte[]); do not keep it afterwards, and do not assume it still holds what you last wrote —
            the same few buffers are cycled as the renderer finishes with them.
            Pixel order is top-down, tightly packed, four bytes per pixel as R, G, B, A.Colour channels must be premultiplied by alpha: the sprite pass treats these as premultiplied, so straight
            alpha reads too bright wherever the image is translucent. Fully opaque and fully transparent pixels are the
            same under both conventions.
Documentation.Returns: A writable buffer, or  if the texture has been disposed.

Documentation.Summary: Length of the buffer M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyGeneratedTexture.BeginUpdate hands out — Size.X * Size.Y * 4.

Hands the filled buffer to the renderer, which replaces the whole image with it and rebuilds the mip chain.
            The buffer belongs to the renderer from here on — write to it again and you will see a torn image.
Pixel format, fixed for the lifetime of the texture.

A toolbar a player can configure: a block's action toolbar, a cockpit's own toolbar, or a
            player's character toolbar. Obtained from a block's T:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbarProvider
            component, and for players from P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyPlayer.CharacterToolbar, which accepts
            writes, or P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyPlayer.Toolbar, the session's read only copy. The inherited
            members address the slots a keyboard player uses; the gamepad slots are a parallel set
            reached through P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbar.GamepadSlots.

The parallel set of slots a gamepad player uses. Null on a character toolbar, which
            has no gamepad slots a player can reach; check for it before use.P:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbarSlots.SlotCount is always four, whatever this toolbar's is,
            because a page maps to the four directions of a pad rather than to the owning block.
            Pages grow as a player fills them and only those up to the last filled slot survive a
            save, so do not store a gamepad slot index between sessions.
Gets a copy of the entire toolbar, including the gamepad slots and the selected slot.
Documentation.Returns: A new object builder describing the toolbar.

Documentation.Summary:
The toolbar's type. Action toolbars are F:VRage.Game.MyToolbarType.ButtonPanel; a
            cockpit's own toolbar reports F:VRage.Game.MyToolbarType.Ship or
            F:VRage.Game.MyToolbarType.Seat, its build toolbar
            F:VRage.Game.MyToolbarType.BuildCockpit, and a character toolbar
            F:VRage.Game.MyToolbarType.Character.

Collects slot assignments for one set of toolbar slots and applies them together. Obtained
            from M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbarSlots.BeginChanges; every method returns the same builder so
            calls can be chained, and nothing happens until M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbarChangeBuilder.Apply.

Applies the batch on the machine that owns these slots, and refuses anywhere else. A
            block toolbar is owned by the server, which applies the change and tells every client
            about it in a single message. A character toolbar is owned by its own player's machine,
            which applies it and lets it reach the session's saved copy from there.So a mod gets itself to the machine that owns the toolbar, by sending its own message,
            and calls this there. A slot the toolbar cannot hold is skipped and the rest still land,
            so a batch can apply in part. The builder is not consumed: keep it and apply it again to
            repeat the same batch.
Documentation.Returns:
True when the batch was applied. False when this machine does not own these
            slots, when the batch was empty, when any call addressed a slot that does not exist or
            named a definition that is not loaded, or when these slots belong to a toolbar the mod
            API cannot write.

Documentation.Summary:
Places an item in a slot, replacing whatever is there. This is what
            M:VRage.Game.ModAPI.IMyToolbarSlots.TryGetItem(System.Int32,VRage.Game.ModAPI.MyToolbarItemInfo@) returns, so a slot read from one toolbar can
            be placed in another as it stands. Any arguments the action takes are dropped; use the
            Set overload in Sandbox.ModAPI to carry them.
Documentation.Returns:
This builder, or a rejected builder when the item names a definition that is
            not loaded.

            gamepad player uses. Both address slots the same way, so code written against this interface
            works on either.

Starts a batch of slot assignments. Chain calls onto the result and finish with

            block toolbar, sends it to clients as one message. Later calls win where two address
            the same slot.

Clears output and fills it with one entry per slot, so that list

Number of slots on a single page.

Runs the item in a slot, as a player pressing it would. A block toolbar is owned by the
            server, so this runs there and refuses anywhere else; a mod gets itself to the server by
            sending its own message and calls this from there. What the item does replicates as
            usual.An item that is not currently available does not run: a block action needs its target
            to share a grid group with the block owning the toolbar.A slot holding a definition rather than an action - a block to build, a tool - selects
            it for whoever is at the keyboard. That is the expected thing in single player and
            nothing useful on a dedicated server, where nobody is.
Documentation.Returns:
True when the item ran. False when this is not the server, when the slot is
            empty or out of range, or when these slots belong to a character toolbar, whose items
            are for the player at the keyboard to select rather than for a mod to fire.

The Curve will evaluate to its first key for positions before the first point in the Curve and to the last key for positions after the last point.
Positions specified past the ends of the curve will wrap around to the opposite side of the Curve.

Positions specified past the ends of the curve will wrap around to the opposite side of the Curve. 
            The value will be offset by the difference between the values of the first and last CurveKey multiplied by the number of times the position wraps around. 
            If the position is before the first point in the Curve, the difference will be subtracted from its value; otherwise, the difference will be added.
Linear interpolation will be performed to determine the value.
Positions specified past the ends of the Curve act as an offset from the same side of the Curve toward the opposite side.
Specifies different tangent types to be calculated for CurveKey points in a Curve.
A Flat tangent always has a value equal to zero.

A Linear tangent at a CurveKey is equal to the difference between its Value and the Value of the preceding or succeeding CurveKey. 
            For example, in Curve MyCurve, where i is greater than zero and (i + 1) is less than the total number of CurveKeys in MyCurve, 
            the linear TangentIn of MyCurve.Keys[i] is equal to: ( MyCurve.Keys[i].Value - MyCurve.Keys[i - 1].Value ) Similarly, 
            the linear TangentOut is equal to: ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Value - MyCurve.Keys[i].Value.)

A Smooth tangent smooths the inflection between a TangentIn and TangentOut by taking into account the values of both neighbors of the CurveKey. 
            The smooth TangentIn of MyCurve.Keys[i] is equal to: ( ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Value - MyCurve.Keys[i - 1].Value ) * 
            ( ( MyCurve.Keys[i].Position - MyCurve.Keys[i - 1].Position ) / ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Position - MyCurve.Keys[i-1].Position ) ) ) 
            Similarly, the smooth TangentOut is equal to: ( ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Value - MyCurve.Keys[i - 1].Value ) * 
            ( ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Position - MyCurve.Keys[i].Position ) / ( MyCurve.Keys[i + 1].Position - MyCurve.Keys[i - 1].Position ) ) )

Documentation.Summary:
A dynamic tree arranges data in a binary tree to accelerate
            queries such as volume queries and ray casts. Leafs are proxies
            with an BoundingBox. In the tree we expand the proxy BoundingBox by Settings.b2_fatAABBFactor
            so that the proxy BoundingBox is bigger than the client object. This allows the client
            object to move by small amounts without triggering a tree update.
            Nodes are pooled and relocatable, so we use node indices rather than pointers.

Default is 1, zero makes billboard - black

Set as F:VRageRender.MyBillboard.ParentID to declare the positions camera-local. The renderer then places the billboard
            with the camera it actually draws that frame with, which is what keeps screen-anchored content pinned —
            positions derived from the game-side camera matrix are a tick stale and swim once the camera is interpolated.

Render object the positions are local to, or F:VRageRender.MyBillboard.PARENT_ID_CAMERA for camera-local ones.
            Unassigned means the positions are absolute world coordinates.
